The three-membered aziridine ring geometry is similar in all conformers, with N-C distances and C-C ring distance in normal ranges, so ring strain is not the main discriminator. The dominant geometric feature is the orientation of the OH group relative to the aziridine N. In the lower-energy geometries, the OH hydrogen points toward N: H...N is about 2.1 to 2.4 A and O...N is about 2.7 to 2.85 A. Using the O-H-N triangle, these also give a reasonably open H-bond angle, roughly 105 to 115 degrees, consistent with a favorable but geometrically constrained intramolecular hydrogen bond. Conformer 19 has one of the shortest H...N distances, around 2.17 A, but the terminal propyl methyl is somewhat close to the OH oxygen, so it is placed very high rather than uniquely first. Conformer 17 has comparable H...N and O...N distances with fewer obvious close methyl contacts, so it is ranked near the top. Conformer 8 is similar, with a short H...N and no severe crowding. Conformer 20 is also in the best group, with H...N near 2.22 A. Conformer 30 is favorable but has the propyl alpha carbon somewhat close to an aziridine carbon, slightly lowering it. Conformer 23 is comparable and slightly less compact. Conformer 5 has a strong H-bond geometry and relatively favorable propyl placement. Conformer 22 and 12 are close in quality, while 15 is similar but slightly weaker in the inferred O-H-N alignment. Conformer 4 has a good H-bond distance and angle but has one propyl CH2 carbon close to N, so it is near the boundary of the top group. Conformers 27, 21, and 13 are favorable intramolecular H-bond structures, but H...N is about 2.35 to 2.36 A; 27 is mildly penalized by the terminal methyl being somewhat close to O. The next tier are still H-bonding but weaker or more bent: 1, 25, 6, 3, 11, 16, 7, and 28. In these, H...N is about 2.5 to 2.65 A and/or the O-H-N angle is more acute. Conformer 1 is relatively unencumbered but has a weaker H-bond than the top group. Conformer 16 has close O...N and H...N contacts but a noticeably bent O-H-N angle, so it is ranked lower than otherwise similar weak H-bonders. Conformers 7 and 28 also have some propyl CH2 contacts toward N. The lowest group lacks an intramolecular O-H...N hydrogen bond: the OH points away from N, with H...N greater than about 3.8 A. These likely have a larger intramolecular dipole and no compensating H-bond. Within this weak-H-bond group, the ordering is mainly by local contacts. Conformer 29 is the least bad because it lacks severe C2...N or C3...O crowding despite the missing H-bond. Conformers 18, 10, and 14 are moderate. Conformer 26 is similar but slightly more crowded. Conformers 2 and 9 have somewhat tighter O contacts to the propyl alpha region. Conformer 24 is placed last because the propyl chain approaches N closely, with a C2...N distance near 2.8 A, combined with the absence of an OH...N hydrogen bond. Overall, the biggest uncertainty is in the middle of the list: weak H-bond conformers and conformers with minor propyl/aziridine steric differences can be reordered by a force field. The separation between the clear H-bonding group and the non-H-bonding group is much more confident than the fine ordering within each group.

Structures with mixed inward/outward vectors were treated as more distorted/twist-like and were placed below the clean chair groups. Within each group, tighter O...methyl or OH H...ring contacts, unusual 1,4 ring distances, and more asymmetric ring geometry were used as penalties. Many mid-ranking entries are subtle and the exact order inside the chair-like groups is uncertain; the broad separation between outward/equatorial, diaxial, and distorted/twist character is more robust.

Two geometric features dominate the estimated stability. (1) An intramolecular O-H...O hydrogen bond is present only in conformers 14 and 9. In 14 the H...O distance is very short (~1.94 A) with O-O ~2.83 A and a nearly linear O-H...O geometry; in 9 it is slightly weaker (~2.09 A, O-O ~2.95 A). Therefore 14 and 9 are expected to be the lowest-energy structures. (2) For the remaining conformers, relief of eclipsing in the fused four-membered rings is the main structural discriminator. I used the out-of-plane puckering of the C7-C9-O-C13 oxetane-like ring and the C5-C7-C13-C15 cyclobutane-like ring as proxies for reduced bond eclipsing. Conformers with more pronounced puckering—especially 27, 22, 15, 13, 1, 2, 21 and 11—are ranked above those with nearly planar four-membered rings, such as 10, 26, 24, 28 and 12. Secondary terms include close nonbonded contacts: when the hydroxyl O is close to the ether O but the H is not donating a hydrogen bond (e.g. 15, 27, 18), a modest O-O repulsion penalty is applied; when the hydroxyl oxygen is too close to the side-chain attachment carbon (O...C5 near or below ~3.0 A), especially in 12, 6, 29, 19 and 21, a steric penalty is applied; and unusually close bridgehead H...H contacts slightly disfavour a few entries (e.g. 12, 5). The middle region is subtler; differences there are likely within a few tenths of a kcal/mol and mainly reflect competing ring puckering, OH rotamer, and weak O...C/O...O contacts. The bottom entries are those with the flattest fused-ring geometries and/or several close contacts. Overall uncertainty is largest outside the top three and in the final five, but the full ordering follows the stated geometric criteria.

These three are ranked first, with 22 and 5 essentially tied and 13 slightly lower because the H...O contact is marginally longer.

Next are strong OH...ether H bonds, where H2...O17 is roughly 2.1 to 2.3 A and O1-O17 is about 2.6 to 2.7 A. Conformer 14 has the shortest H2...O17 contact in this group and very clean side-chain distances. Conformer 15 is similar, with a short H bond and acceptable CH2-CH2 separation. Conformer 7 and 4 both have short H2...O17 contacts and little steric penalty. Conformer 3 has a very short O1-O17 distance, although its H2...O17 distance is slightly longer. Conformer 6 deserves a high position because it appears bifurcated: H2 is close to ether O17 and still within a reasonable weak H-bond distance to the aldehyde O9, with no severe heavy-atom clashes. Conformer 21 has a strong ether H bond but a somewhat close O1-O9 distance, which adds a small O-O repulsive contribution. Conformer 25 is favorable but its H...O17 and O-O distances are slightly longer. Conformer 8 has a comparable ether H bond but slightly tighter O1-C7 and C3-C7 contacts, so it is placed lower in this tier.

A third tier has moderate hydrogen bonding. Conformer 11 has the shortest moderate H2...O17 distance and no serious crowding. Conformer 10 and 12 follow, with H2...O17 about 2.5 to 2.6 A and typical side-chain separations. Conformer 19, 28, and 29 are similar, with H...O around 2.6 A and no severe clashes; 29 is slightly farther in O1-O17 but still acceptable. Conformer 27 has a weaker moderate H bond but noticeably longer side-chain proximity, which is favorable. Conformer 23 and 24 have weak OH...aldehyde interactions, H2...O9 about 2.7 to 2.9 A, and moderately short C3-C7 separations, so they are placed below the moderate ether H-bonded set. Conformer 17 has the weakest hydrogen bond of this tier and is therefore last among the H-bonding structures.

The remaining structures lack a strong intramolecular H bond. They are ranked mainly by absence of steric crowding and favorable oxygen separations. Conformer 9 looks most open, with long side-chain and oxygen separations, so it is placed first among the non-H-bonded set. Conformer 2 is also reasonably open. Conformer 30 has a fairly open aldehyde side chain, though C3-C7 is slightly close. Conformer 18, 26, and 16 have similar, acceptable geometries. Conformer 20 has a slightly tighter C3-C7 contact. Conformer 1 is placed last because it has no H bond, a somewhat close C3-C7 side-chain distance, and a relatively close O1-O9 separation that does not benefit from a hydrogen bond.

Uncertainty is significant. Geometry alone cannot capture ring puckering, torsional strain, dipole alignment, and possible weak dispersion effects. Many structures are separated by small differences, especially within the 14-28, 27-30, 18-26, 16-20, and 1-30 regions. The proposed order is a reasonable chemically based estimate rather than an exact energetic ranking.

reason: All 30 blocks contain the same atom count and a near-cyclopropane C-C-C core with an O-H group attached to one ring carbon and a five-carbon unsaturated side chain on the adjacent ring carbon; the ring itself is rigid, so stability differences are mainly steric and rotational. I ranked structures by minimizing short nonbonded contacts involving the hydroxyl H and the ring CH2/side-chain methylenes, avoiding close O...C contacts to the first side-chain carbon, and favoring side-chain conformations with fewer gauche/syn-pentane contacts. Practical indicators used from the coordinates include: (1) the hydroxyl H should point away from the ring and side chain rather than toward a nearby H or C, (2) the oxygen should be moderately separated from the first side-chain carbon, and (3) the alcohol carbon to terminal side-chain carbon distance should be relatively long, indicating a more extended chain rather than a folded one. Structures such as 17, 21, 3, 20, 16, 8, 13, 23, 25, and 12 combine an outward-pointing OH with an extended side chain, so they are placed highest. The top of the list is not sharply defined because several conformers differ only by small changes in OH orientation and side-chain gauche count. Middle ranked conformers are mostly a trade-off between free OH geometry and a more compact chain, or mildly crowded O...side-chain contacts and a less compact chain. The least stable entries show the worst local crowding: 22 has a very short OH...side-chain H approach with the oxygen also close to the first chain carbon; 9 and 26 also have unfavorable OH...H/side-chain contacts; 4, 6, 24, and 10 are lower because the side chain folds back toward the cyclopropanol ring and the OH or chain hydrogens are brought into the crowded same-side half-space. Differences within the middle group are subtle, so the exact order from about rank 6 to rank 26 is uncertain and mainly reflects small steric/contact penalties rather than large qualitative structural changes.
